title: Delta method
dek: If √n (θ̂ − θ) is asymptotically Normal, then so is g(θ̂), with variance ∇gᵀ Σ ∇g. That is how a SE on the logit becomes a SE on a probability.
story: Labs constantly report functions of fitted parameters: odds ratios e^β, predicted probabilities, attributable fractions, doubling times. The delta method is the first-order Taylor story that turns a covariance matrix for θ̂ into a variance for g(θ̂).

In one dimension, se(g(θ̂)) ≈ |g′(θ̂)| se(θ̂). If g is logit⁻¹, the derivative π(1−π) shrinks SEs near 0 and 1 on the probability scale — which matches Fisher information for Bernoulli, and which is why a tiny SE on π̂ = 0.01 can still sit next to a huge relative error.

The approximation is local and linear. Near boundaries, or when g is highly curved (ratios of small rates), bootstrap or profile likelihood is the grown-up replacement. Delta method is not illegal there; it is just optimistic.
deep: Multivariate: √n (g(θ̂) − g(θ)) →d N(0, ∇gᵀ I₁⁻¹ ∇g) when the MLE is regular and ∇g ≠ 0. If ∇g(θ) = 0, the first-order term vanishes and you need a second-order (often χ²) expansion — classic for variance components tested at 0, which is not a delta-method problem in disguise.
GLM prediction: π̂(x) = g⁻¹(xᵀβ̂). Then ∇_β π = (dg⁻¹/dη) x, and Var(π̂) ≈ (dg⁻¹/dη)² xᵀ Cov(β̂) x. For logit, dg⁻¹/dη = π(1−π). For log-linear Poisson, the mean’s SE scales with μ itself.

Fieller intervals for a ratio a/b when b is near 0 are the classic warning that a linear delta interval can include nonsense or exclude the MLE. Transmission probabilities built as ratios of hazards inherit this.

Invariance of the MLE plus delta method SEs is not the same as transforming a Wald interval endpoint-wise. Endpoint transform of a symmetric Wald interval on ψ = logit(π) is usually better than a Wald interval on π itself.

formulas.label: Multivariate
formulas.note: Plug in ∇g at θ̂. Software calls this the delta method or “using the predict sandwich.”

visual.caption: Error propagating through a map: a nearly Normal law on ψ = logit(π) is pushed through a nonlinear inverse-logit. The gradient |dπ/dψ| = π(1−π) rescales the SE; curvature of the map is what the first-order story ignores.

example.title: SE of an odds ratio
example.setup: Logistic MLE β̂_cav = 1.20 with se = 0.40 for a cavitation coefficient. Scientific report wants OR = e^β and a SE or interval on that scale.

steps.title: Delta SE
steps.body: se(OR̂) ≈ 3.32 × 0.40 ≈ 1.33. A symmetric 3.32 ± 1.96×1.33 includes values near 0.7 and 5.9 and is already feeling the skew of a lognormal.

steps.title: Better report
steps.body: Transform the Wald interval on β: exp(1.20 ± 1.96×0.40) = exp(0.416, 1.984) ≈ (1.52, 7.27). Same first-order ingredients, less symmetric theatre on the OR scale.

example.takeaway: Delta method gives a variance. Transforming an interval on a more Normal scale is often the interval you actually wanted.

check.prompt: If g′(θ) = 0 at the true value, the usual first-order delta method:
choices: Still gives the correct Normal variance
Fails because the linear term vanishes and a higher-order expansion is required
Implies g(θ̂) is super-efficient with variance 0
Is the same as a Bayes delta
check.answer: Fails because the linear term vanishes and a higher-order expansion is required
check.why: The first term in the Taylor expansion of g(θ̂) is g′(θ)(θ̂−θ). Zero gradient means the √n Normal story is the wrong rate.

whyWrong.Implies g(θ̂) is super-efficient with va: A software trap, not a theorem you want.

check.prompt: ψ̂ = −2.0, se(ψ̂) = 0.2, π = logit⁻¹(ψ). Delta-method se(π̂) is closest to:

whyWrong.0.2: That is se on the logit scale.

check.prompt: On the mechanism map, the factor π(1−π) on the last arrow is:
choices: The derivative dπ/dψ that rescales the SE under the delta method
Fisher information for a Poisson mean
check.answer: The derivative dπ/dψ that rescales the SE under the delta method
check.why: d logit⁻¹(ψ)/dψ = π(1−π). That is g′ in se(g) ≈ |g′| se(ψ).
